title: Rain Pooled on a Height Map
statement:
A grid heights describes a block landscape: cell (i, j) is a column of heights[i][j] unit cubes. Rain fills every pocket it can. Water can flow between cells that share a side (up, down, left, right), and any water that reaches a cell on the outer border can flow off the map.

Return the total volume of water that stays on the map.

examples.why: The two inner cells are walled in at height 3: 2 + 3 = 5.
The wall has a low spot of 2 on the right edge. Water rises to 2, not 4, so the center holds 1.
The three low cells drain through the 2 on the bottom edge, so each holds 1. Checking each row and column on its own would see walls of 5.

hints: In one dimension the level at a cell was the lower of the two tallest walls. In 2D, what decides how high water at a cell can rise?
Water at a cell escapes along the path to the border whose highest point is lowest. The level is that path's highest point.
Start from the whole border in a min-heap and always expand from the lowest boundary cell. A neighbor's level is max(its height, the level of the cell you came from); push it with that level.

explain.intuition:
Water at a cell rises until it finds a way out. Every route to the border has a highest point it must climb over, and water takes the route where that highest point is lowest. So the level at a cell is the minimum, over all escape routes, of the route's maximum height. The two-pointer trick from the 1D version doesn't carry over, because routes can turn corners.

Think of the border as a dam and flood inward from its lowest point, like Dijkstra's algorithm. Keep the current boundary in a min-heap by level. The lowest boundary cell is the weakest point in the wall: any unvisited neighbor of it must drain through it or through something at least as high, so its level is max(own height, that boundary level). Add the difference to the total and push the neighbor as part of the new boundary.
steps: Push every border cell with level = its height and mark it visited.
Pop the lowest cell (level, i, j).
For each unvisited neighbor: add max(0, level − height) to the total, mark it visited and push it with level max(level, height).
Repeat until the heap is empty; return the total.
pitfalls: Taking min(row walls, column walls) per cell as in 1D. Water escapes around corners, as in the third example.
Pushing a neighbor with its own height instead of max(level, height). A low cell behind a low cell would then leak too much.
Forgetting to mark border cells visited, so they get filled as if they were interior.

solutions.title: Lower levels until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Start every inner cell at an infinite level and the border at its height. Repeatedly set each inner cell to max(height, lowest neighbor level) until a full pass changes nothing.

solutions.title: Flood inward from the border with a min-heap
solutions.idea: The border is the first wall. Always grow from its lowest cell: each new neighbor's level is max(its height, that wall level).

followups: Return the water depth for each cell instead of the total.
Heights are small integers (say, at most 100). Replace the heap with buckets. What is the new running time?
